content.body:
I had already pooped three times before our Santorini excursion.

But my husband was still standing beside the cabin door with our tickets while I waited for the pressure in my belly to come back.

Every time I stood up, I felt as if the bowel movement had stopped halfway through.

The ship's doctor asked me one question my gastroenterologist had never asked.

"How many of those bowel movements actually feel complete?"

I'm 56 years old.

My husband and I saved for two years for this cruise.

Two weeks through the Mediterranean.

Greece, Italy and Spain.

Day four was Santorini.

We had paid for the excursion months earlier.

My husband was dressed and standing beside the cabin door with our tickets.

I was sitting on the toilet for the third time that morning.

The first portion had come out before breakfast.

It looked normal enough that I washed my hands and assumed I was done.

Twenty minutes later, a dull pressure returned low in my belly.

I went back and passed a much smaller portion.

But when I stood up, I still did not feel empty.

So I sat down again and pushed harder.

Almost nothing came out.

I could go.

I just couldn't trust that I was finished.

"Give me another twenty minutes," I called through the bathroom door.

My husband did not complain.

That somehow made me feel worse.

He sat on the edge of the bed with our tickets while I walked between the bathroom and the cabin door waiting for another urge.

Eventually, the excursion could not wait for my body.

I picked up my bag and left with the same pressure under my waistband.

Santorini was exactly as beautiful as the photographs.

White buildings.

Blue roofs.

The sea below us.

But I spent the morning checking where the nearest restroom was.

Every time the pressure became stronger, I wondered whether I needed to find a bathroom again.

My belly became more swollen as the morning went on.

I loosened the button inside my skirt and kept walking.

That was the fourth morning of the cruise that had started the same way.

Two or three attempts.

No clean feeling that the movement had actually ended.

And another piece of the trip spent planning around a bathroom.

When we returned to the ship, my husband put the tickets on the dresser.

"This is taking over the trip," he said.

He was right.

At home, nobody saw it.

I could get up early, make another attempt and quietly wait near my own bathroom.

On the ship, every breakfast, excursion and departure time made the problem visible.

My husband had watched me put down my bag and return to the bathroom four mornings in a row.

"Please talk to the doctor," he said.

I did not want to explain this to a stranger.

I had already told my gastroenterologist about the repeat trips and lingering pressure.

But our conversations always came back to how often I went and what I was taking.

I always answered, "Every morning."

That answer made the problem sound smaller than it felt.

But I had spent two years saving for this cruise.

I did not want to spend the rest of it waiting beside a cabin bathroom.

The next morning, I went to the ship's concierge.

She found me an appointment that afternoon.

The medical office was small and clean.

Deck 3, near the center of the ship.

Dr. Weber had an Austrian accent and looked to be in her mid-fifties.

She examined my abdomen and asked where I felt the pressure.

Then she sat across from me with a pen.

"When was your last bowel movement?" she asked.

"This morning," I said.

"Three times."

She looked up.

"Three complete bowel movements?"

I hesitated.

"I don't know."

She asked me to describe exactly what happened.

So I told her about the normal-looking first portion.

The pressure returning over breakfast.

The smaller second portion.

The third attempt that sometimes produced almost nothing.

I told her that the pressure could stay with me until lunch.

I told her about the trapped gas and the waistband I kept loosening.

Then she asked the question that changed everything.

"How many of those movements actually feel complete?"

I laughed because the answer sounded ridiculous once I said it aloud.

"Maybe one a week."

She put down her pen.

"Then you are counting bathroom visits," she said.

"You are not counting complete bowel movements."

Before working in ship medicine, Dr. Weber had spent years in a GI motility clinic in Austria.

She had heard this pattern before.

She called it incomplete evacuation.

Then she explained what she could and could not know from my symptoms.

The repeated portions, bloating and pressure suggested that the movement was not carrying through cleanly.

She said she had seen that combination of fragmented output, trapped gas and lingering pressure in some patients with elevated methane.

"When you get home, ask your gastroenterologist for a methane breath test," she said.

She wrote the name of the test on a piece of paper.

Underneath it, she wrote four things for me to track.

How many bathroom visits it took before I felt finished.

Whether I ever felt completely empty.

How much time passed between the first portion and the end of the movement.

And whether the pressure followed me into breakfast or out of the house.

Just a better question, a test to request and a way to describe what my mornings were actually costing me.

For the rest of the cruise, I kept thinking about the difference between going and finishing.

Seven years.

My gastroenterologist had asked how often I went.

She had recommended more water, fiber and MiraLAX.

I had answered, "Every morning."

Neither of us had stopped to measure whether those mornings ever ended with relief.

When we returned to Boston, I called her office.

"The ship's doctor told me to ask for a methane breath test," I said.

The test kit arrived with instructions for the day before.

On the morning of the test, I drank the solution and breathed into a series of collection bags over the next few hours.

The test cost me nearly $300, and collecting all the carefully timed breath samples took most of the morning.

When the report came back, my gastroenterologist scheduled a call.

"Your methane reached 28 parts per million," she said.

"The laboratory marks 10 or more as methane-positive."

Twenty-eight parts per million.

The laboratory threshold was ten.

For the first time, I had something more objective than pressure, guesses and another morning near the toilet.

My gastroenterologist explained that the positive result could fit a slower-movement pattern.

Then she asked what I wanted to do next.

I told her I needed a few days to understand what the result meant before I added another remedy to my shelf.

That night, I opened my laptop at 11:45.

My first search was simple.

"methane positive breath test constipation"

Then I searched:

"methane slow intestinal movement"

"why poop comes out in separate portions"

"methane incomplete evacuation"

At 1:30 in the morning, I was still reading.

I did not understand every scientific term.

I did not try to pretend that I did.

But I kept finding one connection that made my own mornings finally make sense.

Higher methane was associated with slower movement through the gut.

In my own words, it acted like a brake.

I pictured the conveyor belt at a grocery-store checkout.

The belt could start moving and carry the first few groceries toward the cashier.

Then it could slow before the rest reached the end.

The first groceries arriving did not mean the whole order had arrived.

The belt still had to keep moving.

That was what my three bathroom trips felt like.

The first portion came out because the movement started.

The pressure remained because it had not finished.

When another weaker wave came twenty minutes later, I returned and passed a little more.

If a third wave came, I made a third trip.

If it did not, I carried that unfinished pressure into breakfast and through the rest of the morning.

That was why I could poop three times and still feel constipated.

Once I understood that, I went back through everything I had tried.

Water sometimes made the first portion easier to pass.

MiraLAX drew more water into the stool and sometimes made that first portion softer and larger.

But softer output was not the same as a movement that continued until I felt empty.

Fiber gave the slowed movement more material to carry and often left me more bloated.

Magnesium could loosen the stool without guaranteeing that the movement would finish.

Senna and Dulcolax could create urgency and extra trips, but the same unfinished pattern returned after the temporary force wore off.

For years, I had treated each remedy as another way to make more come out.

More water to soften it.

More fiber to enlarge it.

More magnesium to loosen it.

More stimulant to force it.

But the result I wanted was not more output.

It was one bowel movement that began and finished.

The next evening, I started with a question I had not known to ask before.

"what produces methane inside the gut"

That was when I learned that methane came from microbes called methanogens living among the larger community inside the gut.

They used material left behind by other microbes.

The more active they became, the more methane they could produce.

So I searched again.

"methanogens gut microbial balance"

"support beneficial gut bacteria polyphenols"

That trail led me repeatedly to plant compounds called polyphenols.

One group of those compounds was called anthocyanins.

They were the dark red, blue and purple pigments found in certain plants.

What caught my attention was that some of those compounds can continue into the lower gut, where they interact with the microbial community.

I kept reading about the possibility that they could help beneficial bacteria compete in that environment.

I need to be clear about what I found.

I did not find a paper promising that one cup of ordinary tea would cure every case of constipation.

I found a direction that made sense alongside my positive methane test.

Support the microbial balance.

Reduce the advantage methane-producing microbes had gained.

Potentially ease part of the brake on movement.

Give the bowel movement a better chance to continue beyond the first portion.

Then I compared foods and drinks that contained the compounds I had written down.

That was what kept bringing me back to hibiscus.

Its deep-red flowers contained the anthocyanins and polyphenols I had been reading about, and I could brew them into a concentrated daily drink.

The dark color was not simply decoration.

It was a visible clue that the pigment was still present.

But the more I searched, the more I realized that the word hibiscus on the front of a box told me almost nothing about what was inside.

Anthocyanin pigments can be affected by heat, air, rough processing and long storage.

Crushing a flower into small pieces exposes more of it to those conditions.

Blending a little hibiscus with rosehips, peppermint, flavoring and other herbs can make water look red without providing the amount of hibiscus I thought I was buying.

Dark, intact flowers gave me a visible sign that the pigment had not already disappeared into old tea dust.

Organic growing reduced the question of what had been sprayed onto something I planned to brew every day.

High-altitude growing mattered because stronger sunlight can encourage the plant to make more protective pigment.

Hand-picking allowed deeper-red flowers to be selected instead of harvesting everything for volume.

Careful drying helped preserve the dark color after the flowers were picked.

And a concentrated deep-ruby brew gave me one final visible check in my cup.

So I wrote down five requirements.

Organic whole flowers.

High-altitude grown.

Hand-picked.

Carefully dried.

A concentrated deep-ruby brew.

Then I did what I always did when a simple solution sounded expensive.

I tried to save money.

The grocery store eight minutes from our house had a bright red box with a hibiscus flower on the front.

It cost $3.79.

I told myself hibiscus was hibiscus.

I opened the box at my kitchen table.

The bags contained pale crushed pieces mixed with other herbs.

The tea turned pinkish red instead of deep ruby.

But I had already paid for it.

So I decided to test it properly.

Every morning, I recorded how many bathroom visits it took before I felt finished.

I recorded whether I ever felt completely empty.

I recorded how many minutes passed between the first portion and the end of the movement.

And I recorded whether the pressure followed me into breakfast or out of the house.

I drank two cups of the grocery-store tea every day for 21 days.

One with breakfast.

One after dinner.

During the first seven days, I needed three bathroom visits on five mornings and two visits on the other two.

Not one of those seven mornings felt completely finished.

During the second seven days, I made 18 bathroom trips.

Only one morning ended with a complete feeling.

The pressure followed me into breakfast on five mornings and out of the house on three.

During the final seven days, I made 19 bathroom trips.

Only one morning felt complete.

The process still consumed between 90 minutes and three hours.

At the end of 21 days, I turned the box over.

Hibiscus.

Rosehips.

Lemongrass.

Peppermint.

Natural flavor.

The tea was red.

But I had not bought the dark whole flowers described in my research.

I had bought a flavored blend that happened to contain some hibiscus.

The flowers were not whole.

They were not dark and intact.

There was no high-altitude growing or hand-picking information.

The brew was not deep ruby.

And the hibiscus was blended with four other ingredients.

So I narrowed my search to products that met every requirement.

That was how I found PiPi Tea.

PiPi Tea used organic whole hibiscus flowers.

The flowers were high-altitude grown.

They were hand-picked.

They were carefully dried to preserve their dark pigment.

They were dark, intact and nothing like the pale dust in the tea bags I had just finished.

When brewed, they produced the concentrated deep-ruby cup I had been trying to find.

I ordered PiPi Tea from https://shop.pipitea.com/hbt/kd/c/sp-nm.

It arrived three days later.

I opened the bag at my kitchen table.

The first thing I noticed was that I could see the flowers.

They were whole.

They were dark red.

They looked nothing like the powder I had steeped for three weeks.

I brewed one cup the next morning.

The water turned deep ruby in three minutes.

I drank it with breakfast.

I brewed another cup after dinner.

And I continued using the same notebook.

During my final seven days using the grocery-store tea, I had made 19 bathroom trips.

Only one of those seven mornings ended with a complete feeling.

The process usually consumed between 90 minutes and three hours.

The pressure followed me into breakfast on five mornings and out of the house on three.

Here is exactly what happened next.

PiPi Week 1 was not dramatic.

I made 17 bathroom trips across seven mornings.

I needed three trips on three mornings and two trips on the other four.

Two of the seven mornings eventually felt complete.

The pressure followed me into breakfast on four mornings and out of the house on three.

PiPi Week 2 was the first time the pattern clearly shifted.

I made 13 bathroom trips across seven mornings.

Four mornings needed two trips.

One morning needed three.

On Thursday and Sunday, I went once and stood up feeling empty.

Four of the seven mornings felt complete that week.

The pressure followed me beyond breakfast on three mornings instead of five.

PiPi Week 3 was when I started to believe this was different.

I made ten bathroom trips across seven mornings.

Four mornings ended after one visit.

Three mornings needed two visits.

Five of the seven mornings felt complete.

The average time between the first portion and feeling finished fell from nearly two hours to 34 minutes.

The pressure followed me out of the house twice.

PiPi Week 4 was the week I began trusting the complete feeling.

I made eight bathroom trips across seven mornings.

Six mornings ended after one visit.

One morning needed a second trip.

Six of the seven mornings felt complete.

The pressure followed me beyond breakfast once that entire week.

On Friday, I stood up after one visit and felt no returning pressure.

Normally, I would still have waited twenty minutes just in case.

That morning, I got dressed, picked up my bag and left the house with my husband.

I did not put the bag down again.

The next month was not perfect, but the improvement held.

By PiPi Week 8, 20 of 28 mornings ended after one bathroom visit.

Twenty-four of those 28 mornings felt complete.

Seven mornings needed a second visit.

One difficult morning still needed three.

The pressure followed me out of the house on three of those 28 mornings.

I used MiraLAX four times across those four weeks instead of roughly 20 times.

By PiPi Week 12, I had recorded 25 complete mornings out of 28.

Twenty-two ended after one visit.

Five needed a second visit.

One needed three.

Three mornings still felt incomplete.

But not one of the 28 disappeared into a three-hour wait.

The pressure followed me beyond breakfast twice.

At three months, I returned to my gastroenterologist with the notebook.

She reviewed the methane report first.

Then she looked at the numbers I had tracked.

She circled the 19 bathroom trips before PiPi Tea.

Then she circled eight trips in Week 4.

Then she circled 22 one-visit mornings in my final 28 days.

Finally, she circled the 25 mornings that had ended with a complete feeling.

"This is a meaningful change in the complaint you actually came in with," she said.

"Not simply going more often."

"Finishing."

I stopped counting how many times I went.

I started noticing whether I felt finished.

My gastroenterologist had not been hiding the question from me.

She had asked about frequency because that was how I had always described the problem.

Dr. Weber had given me a different question.

The breath test gave me the number.

And my own research finally helped me understand why the distinction mattered.

I turned 57 later that year.

I still go to the bathroom most mornings.

The difference is that now, most mornings, I go once.

I stand up feeling empty.

I wash my hands and leave the bathroom without waiting for another wave.

Last month, my husband and I spent a weekend near the coast.

On Saturday morning, we had tickets for the first ferry.

I went to the bathroom once before breakfast.

Twelve minutes later, I stood up feeling empty.

My husband was beside the hotel door holding the tickets.

I picked up my bag and walked toward him.

I did not put it down.

He looked at me for a second.

"You're not waiting anymore," he said.

I had not realized he remembered those mornings on the cruise as clearly as I did.

I don't get anything from sharing this.

I just know what it is like to make three bathroom trips and still leave feeling unfinished.

If you go every morning but still stand up feeling as if you never completely emptied your bowels, you know what I mean.

You know the first trip that looks successful.

You know the pressure that returns after you wash your hands.

You know the smaller second portion.

You know the third attempt that produces almost nothing.

You know what it is to keep asking for another twenty minutes.

You know the bloating and trapped gas that follow you after the bathroom.

And you know the frustration of making more come out without ever getting the complete relief you wanted.

The number of times you sit on the toilet is not the same as the number of complete bowel movements you have.

Three visits can still be one unfinished movement.

In my case, testing showed methane at 28 parts per million against a laboratory threshold of ten.

That result gave me a reason to investigate why my movement kept losing force before the end.

That is why the anthocyanins and polyphenols mattered to me.

They were not there to create one more violent flush.

I chose them to support the microbial environment I had been researching.

Support a healthier microbial balance.

Make the environment less favorable to methane-producing microbes.

Potentially reduce methane activity.

Ease part of the braking pressure on the colon's contractions.

Give the movement a better chance to carry through to the finish.

But the quality of the hibiscus mattered.

I learned that after wasting 21 days on a $3.79 blended tea bag.

PiPi Tea uses organic whole hibiscus flowers.

P.S. My husband took a photograph of me in Santorini.

The white buildings and blue water were behind me.

But I was turned halfway back toward the restroom sign with one hand pressed below my waistband.

Last month, he took another photograph while we waited for the ferry near the coast.

My bag was already over my shoulder.

I was looking toward the water instead of back toward the hotel bathroom.

He showed me the two photographs side by side.
